# Core Decor Reel Automation — reference for AI tools

This file exists so any AI assistant picking up this repo — a fresh Claude session,
another tool, whatever — has the context that took real trial-and-error to establish,
without re-deriving it from scratch or repeating mistakes already caught once.

## Starting a new chat? Paste this to the new AI first

Copy-paste this whole block as your first message in a new conversation, with any
AI assistant, to pick up exactly where things left off:

> I'm continuing work on an automated social media pipeline for my business Core
> Decor. The repo is https://github.com/devdave666/core-decor-automation (public).
> Read `llms.txt` at the repo root first, in full — it has the architecture, every
> bug that's already been found and fixed (don't re-diagnose these), current status,
> and exactly what access you need from me to actually work on this (see the "Giving
> a new AI agent access" section in that same file). Once you've read it, tell me
> what you understand the current state to be, then I'll tell you what I need today.

That's it — everything else the new AI needs is in this file, not in your head.

## What this project does

Builds Reels for Core Decor from an audio track plus a library of 50 AI-generated
"swatch" (material flat-lay) and "application" (finished room) image pairs, then
publishes the same finished video to **four platforms**: Instagram and Facebook via
the direct Meta Graph API, TikTok and YouTube via Buffer (direct-API integration for
those two was judged too high-friction — TikTok's app review, YouTube's OAuth
verification — so Buffer's free tier is used as a pragmatic shortcut instead). Runs
unattended daily via GitHub Actions, no human step required in the normal case. Core
files:

- `core_decor_reel_pipeline.py` — the whole pipeline: audio mastering, cut-timing
  extraction, video compositing, publishing to all four platforms.
- `caption_bank.py` — modular hook/CTA/hashtag pools combined deterministically for
  hundreds of unique captions, cycled via `caption_index.txt` (committed to the repo,
  same pattern as `day_counter.txt` in the `millionchallenge` repo). No LLM call, no
  runtime cost.
- `media/reels/` — finished reels land here and are served via
  `raw.githubusercontent.com` for Meta and Buffer to both fetch from. **This repo
  must stay public** for that URL to work (raw content links don't serve private
  repos). Nothing secret is ever in repo *content* — secrets only ever live in
  GitHub Actions' encrypted secrets store, which is unaffected by repo visibility.
- `.github/workflows/daily-reel.yml` — the primary schedule, 14:00 UTC daily.
- `.github/workflows/missed-post-check.yml` — safety net, 20:00 UTC daily; checks
  whether today's primary run actually succeeded and auto-triggers a recovery run
  if not. See "Missed-run recovery" below for why this exists.
- `hot_takes/` — a SECOND, entirely separate content type (opinion/meme-text over
  a single application photo, no swatch, no reveal). Own schedule, own state,
  reuses this pipeline's publishing/hosting code without modifying any of it.
  See "Hot Takes" below — don't assume the swatch+application description above
  applies to it, it deliberately doesn't.
- `concept_tools/` — asset PREP, not runtime: builds the image pairs the
  pipelines later consume. Includes the in-progress **d-series** three-band
  concept format, which is currently IMAGE GENERATION ONLY and deliberately not
  connected to any publishing. See "The d-series" below before touching it.
- `carousel_post/` — a FOURTH content type: a static two-image carousel
  (c-series swatch, then its own application shot), twice a week. No video, no
  audio, no ffmpeg. See "Carousel Post" below — don't assume anything
  video/Reels-specific above applies to it.

## Cut-timing approach: read this before touching anything beat-related

Three approaches were tried, in this order, for real reasons:

1. **Beat tracking on every beat** (`extract_beat_timestamps`, using
   `librosa.beat.beat_track`) — cuts on every detected beat. Worked mathematically
   (verified cuts landed within one video frame of computed boundaries) but the
   human verdict was "feels random, independent of the music." Detected beats being
   mathematically correct doesn't mean they're musically satisfying — this is the
   core lesson, not a bug to re-litigate.
2. **Impact-beat reveal structure** (`extract_impact_beats` +
   `build_reveal_reel`) — cuts only on the 4 most acoustically strong hits, structured
   as swatch-holds-then-reveals-on-the-hit rather than continuous alternation. Better,
   but still algorithmic, still occasionally off from what actually sounds right.
3. **Template timing** (`extract_template_cut_timestamps` +
   `build_reel_from_template_timing`) — the current approach. Extracts the exact cut
   timestamps from a reference reel the user already made and is happy with (via
   ffmpeg scene detection, not PySceneDetect — deliberately, see below), then applies
   that exact pattern to fresh audio and image pairs. Sidesteps "is this
   algorithmically-detected beat actually musical" entirely by copying proven-good
   timing instead of re-deriving it.

**Do not silently revert to approach 1 or 2 as "simpler."** They were tried and
found wanting on human judgment, not on math. If picking a method, default to 3.

**On PySceneDetect vs raw ffmpeg scene filter:** research suggested PySceneDetect as
the "cleanest" method. Went with the raw ffmpeg `select='gt(scene,X)',showinfo` filter
instead — deliberately, not out of laziness — because that exact method was already
validated earlier in this project (matched computed segment boundaries to real scene
cuts within one frame) and adding PySceneDetect would mean a new dependency for
something already proven. Don't add it without a concrete reason the ffmpeg filter
can't handle.

## Known audio gotchas

- **Instagram sometimes appends a short outro jingle** to downloaded audio — loud,
  arrhythmic, no real periodicity. `beat_track` fits ONE tempo across the whole
  signal, so a few seconds of this at the tail can drag the entire track's estimate
  off, not just its own segment (confirmed: removing one measured outro shifted a
  track's detected tempo from 117.2 to 119.7 BPM and dropped 6 beats that had been
  landing inside the noise). Automatic detection/trimming for this was built, then
  **removed by explicit request** — the user will supply outro-free tracks going
  forward. If that stops holding, the fix is straightforward to reinstate: scan the
  back half of the track for a sustained quiet RMS gap, trim to it before mastering.
- **Octave errors are real**: `beat_track` can mistake a tempo for its double or
  half. `_correct_octave_error()` re-tracks with a biased `start_bpm` prior if the
  raw estimate falls outside a plausible 70–160 BPM range. Don't just relabel the
  reported number — the actual beat *positions* need re-tracking with the corrected
  prior, or they stay aligned to the wrong tempo.
- **Frame-accurate cut boundaries matter**: duration-based clip assembly can
  accumulate sub-frame rounding drift across many concatenated clips. Boundaries are
  snapped to exact frame multiples (`round(t * fps) / fps`) before any duration is
  computed, not after.

## Explicitly rejected: audio fingerprint alteration

An early spec for this pipeline called for a sub-semitone pitch shift decoupled from
tempo, plus noise injected below the audible threshold, framed as altering the
track's "acoustic fingerprint" while keeping it "pleasant to human ears." That
combination is the standard technique for evading content-matching systems (Meta's
own Rights Manager among them) — it was not built, on purpose, regardless of how a
future request frames it. Stage 1 does ordinary mastering only: an EQ shelf and
loudness normalization to -14 LUFS (Instagram/Spotify's own standard target).

## MoviePy version note

This project uses **MoviePy 2.x**, which has a different API from 1.x: no
`moviepy.editor` submodule (import directly from `moviepy`), and `.resize()` /
`.crop()` / `.set_duration()` / `.set_audio()` were renamed to `.resized()` /
`.cropped()` / `.with_duration()` / `.with_audio()`. If code examples online use the
old names, they're for MoviePy 1.x — don't copy them in verbatim.

## Image pairing

Swatch and application images are matched by filename prefix
(`c01_kit_modlux_swatch.png` ↔ `c01_kit_modlux_app.png`), never pooled independently.
An earlier version pulled from two separate cycles over the full image pool, which let
any swatch land next to any unrelated concept's application shot — `_pair_swatches_
with_applications()` fixed this. Any new compositing function must preserve
same-concept pairing; this was a real, verified-on-video bug, not a style preference.

## Facebook video publishing — RESOLVED. Read this before touching publish_to_facebook again.

`publish_to_facebook()` now uses the dedicated **Reels Publishing API**
(`/{page_id}/video_reels`, pull-based via a `file_url` header on rupload.facebook.com)
— NOT the general Video API's push-based Resumable Upload, which this project used
for a long time and which never worked reliably for this content. If you're tempted
to "simplify" this back to the general `/videos` endpoint with a push upload: don't,
without rereading this whole section and re-running the elimination tests below.

### The actual root cause, isolated by systematic elimination, not a guess

The general Video API's push-based upload silently truncated CONCATENATED video
content server-side, while reporting complete success. Confirmed on real published
posts, delivered `length` came back as 1.7s, then 1.7s again, then 4s, then 10s, then
4.8s — against source files that were actually ~20s — across a dozen combinations of
encoding parameters, upload chunking strategies, and even different HTTP client
implementations (`requests` vs raw `curl`). Every single attempt returned a normal
success response with no error anywhere in the chain; the only thing that ever caught
it was polling the delivered video's own reported `length` afterward.

Isolating the actual variable took building a deliberate ladder of test videos and
testing each one for real against the live API:
- A single continuous-source video (flat color, or one static photo held for the
  full duration) — ANY size, ANY duration — delivered correctly, every time, no
  exceptions, across half a dozen tests.
- A video built by CONCATENATING multiple distinct clips — even just 4 short clips,
  even at under 2MB total, far smaller than anything that had failed before —
  truncated unpredictably, regardless of which tool built the concatenation
  (MoviePy's re-encode `concatenate_videoclips`, or ffmpeg's raw stream-copy concat
  demuxer) and regardless of keyframe strategy (default scene-triggered keyframes,
  or forced regular GOP intervals via `-x264-params scenecut=0:keyint=60` — tested
  explicitly to rule out a keyframe-density theory, which turned out to be wrong).

Conclusion: it's concatenation itself hitting some defect in the general Video API's
push-upload handling — not file size, not duration, not a specific encoder setting.
Meta's own Reels spec requires "Closed GOP (2-5 seconds)"; a reel with a cut (and
therefore a fresh keyframe) every 0.3-5 seconds likely violates that, though the
EXACT mechanism inside Meta's infrastructure was never confirmed — only that
avoiding the push-upload path entirely made the problem disappear completely.

### The fix

Switched to the Reels-specific pull-based flow: start a session
(`POST /{page_id}/video_reels`, `upload_phase: start`), have Meta PULL the file from
a URL we already host (`POST` to the returned `upload_url` on `rupload.facebook.com`
with a `file_url` header — no bytes pushed at all), confirm the server's own
`bytes_transferred` matches the real file size, then finish
(`POST /{page_id}/video_reels`, `upload_phase: finish`, `video_state: PUBLISHED`).
Tested against the exact same real 19.85s production reel that had just been
truncated to 4s via the push method, with no other change — it delivered
`length: 19.805`, fully processed, fully published, verified via
`_verify_facebook_video_duration()`. That's why the old implementation was replaced
outright, not kept as a fallback.

Same permissions as before — `pages_show_list`, `pages_read_engagement`,
`pages_manage_posts` — no new grant needed for this switch.

### The separate, real permission problem this also depended on solving

Error `(#100) No permission to publish the video` was a genuinely different, earlier
problem, now also resolved. It looked like a missing grant, and burned real time on
two wrong turns (a Business-type app has no Development/Live mode concept at all —
don't send anyone looking for that toggle) before landing on the actual cause:
`pages_manage_posts` sat at "Ready for testing" access, which only works for people
with an actual role (Admin/Developer/Tester) on the app itself — a system-user token
doesn't count as having a role the way a personal admin's token does, even though
Business Settings showed it with "Full Access" to the Page.

**The permanent fix**: derive a long-lived Page token from a PERSONAL user login,
not the system user. `GET /me/accounts?fields=access_token,tasks` using a long-lived
user token (itself obtained via the standard `fb_exchange_token` grant) returns a
Page access token with `expires_at: 0` — genuinely permanent, not the ~1-hour token
Graph API Explorer hands out directly. Confirm `CREATE_CONTENT` appears in that
Page's `tasks` list before trusting it. This is what's stored in the
`META_SYSTEM_USER_TOKEN` secret now — the name is a historical artifact (it started
as an actual system-user token before this fix); it now holds this personally-derived
Page token instead. Don't be misled by the variable name into regenerating a fresh
system-user token and reintroducing the permission problem.

This token relies on the underlying Facebook account's login staying valid — it has
no fixed expiry, but changing that account's password would invalidate it. Business
Verification (real business name/address/documents, reviewed by Meta) is the more
"proper" alternative if that becomes a problem, deliberately avoided here per an
explicit preference to keep personal/business information exposure minimal.

## Hot Takes — second content type, fully separate from everything above

Everything above this section describes the ORIGINAL content type: swatch, then
its own application shot, cycling through image pairs with cut-timing copied from
a template. Hot Takes is a second, deliberately different format added later,
living entirely in `hot_takes/` — nothing above this section changed to
accommodate it, verified via `git diff core_decor_reel_pipeline.py` before and
after adding it.

**Why it exists**: real view-count data showed a separate, hand-made batch of
meme-style content ("They: Let's just paint the walls." / "Me: No…" text over a
single room photo) dramatically outperforming the swatch+application format —
200-580 views vs. single digits on the same account, same window. That gap is
almost certainly about hook/format, not about API-vs-manual publishing — the
swatch+application format has no mechanism for a punchy opinion-driven hook at
all, so of course a format built around one performs differently. Hot Takes
brings that hook-driven approach into the automated pipeline rather than
requiring it to stay manual forever.

**What it actually is**: ONE application photo (no swatch, no multi-image
reveal, no cut-timing extraction from a template) held for a short duration
(≤7s — meme pacing is short and punchy, not a slow reveal arc), with a two-line
"setup / punchline" text overlay that appears in sequence — the setup line alone
first, the punchline 1.6s later. Rendered via PIL onto transparent PNGs (white
text, black stroke, the standard meme-text convention) and composited with
MoviePy — deliberately not MoviePy's own TextClip, which depends on ImageMagick
being correctly configured; PIL has no such dependency.

**Files**: `hot_takes/hot_takes_pipeline.py` (build + publish), `opinion_bank.py`
(the setup/punchline content pool, same fixed-pool-cycled-deterministically
philosophy as caption_bank.py one level up — no LLM call), `text_overlay.py`
(the PIL rendering). State: `application_index.txt`, `opinion_index.txt`,
`caption_index.txt`, `template_index.txt` — all four living inside `hot_takes/`,
not at the repo root, and this is load-bearing, not cosmetic: `core.
get_next_caption_and_index`/`advance_caption_index` and `core.fetch_next_template`
hardcode the MAIN pipeline's own root-level counter files internally. Calling
them directly from Hot Takes would have both pipelines racing on the same
shared pointer whenever they happen to run close together. Hot Takes has its
own small equivalents (`_get_next_caption`, `_fetch_template_for_audio`) that
reuse the underlying content (caption_bank's pool, the same Drive Template Reels
folder) but track position independently. If extending Hot Takes, or adding a
third content type, check for this pattern before reusing any counter-adjacent
helper from the main pipeline — reusing the CONTENT is fine and encouraged;
reusing the COUNTER FILE silently is the actual danger.

**A real bug worth knowing about if touching the image-compositing code again**:
the background image render came out completely black on the first real test.
Cause: `bg = bg.resized(scale).cropped(x_center=bg.w/2, ...)` written as one
chained expression — `bg.w` inside that expression evaluates against the OLD
un-resized clip, not the resized one, because Python evaluates the entire
right-hand side before the reassignment happens. Fixed by splitting into two
statements (`bg = bg.resized(scale)` then `bg = bg.cropped(x_center=bg.w/2,
...)` on its own line) — matching how the main pipeline's own image-compositing
code already does it correctly, elsewhere in this file. Caught by inspecting
the actual composite frame's pixel data directly rather than assuming a visually
"reasonable-looking" code change worked.

**Publishing**: reuses `publish_to_instagram`, `publish_to_facebook`,
`publish_to_buffer`, `upload_video_to_public_host`, and the generic
`_read_counter`/`_write_and_commit_counter` helpers directly from
`core_decor_reel_pipeline.py` via import — genuinely shared, no reimplementation.
Hosted at `media/hot_takes/` (a different subdirectory than the main pipeline's
`media/reels/`, passed via `upload_video_to_public_host`'s existing
`media_subdir` parameter — already fully parameterized, no changes needed there).

**Schedule**: `.github/workflows/hot-takes-reel.yml`, every 2 days at 18:00 UTC —
independent of the main pipeline's 14:00 UTC daily schedule, so the two formats
don't both land the same day by default. Both the cadence and the time are
placeholders, same as the main schedule's own 14:00 UTC choice — revisit once
there's engagement data.

**Verified end-to-end on a real live run** (not just built and assumed working):
real post IDs confirmed on all four platforms, the actual delivered video
downloaded and visually checked frame-by-frame (both the setup-alone frame and
the punchline-revealed frame), and all four Hot-Takes-specific counters
confirmed to advance correctly while the main pipeline's own counters were
confirmed unchanged by the same run.

### Four real refinements made after the first version shipped

The first version worked but wasn't good enough — real, substantive feedback,
not cosmetic nitpicks. All four fixed and re-verified against a real live post
before considering this done again:

1. **Opinion bank referenced specific colors/materials** ("Beige is boring",
   "That's a lot of brass for one room") — but the pipeline has zero attribute
   awareness; it cycles through application photos with no idea what's actually
   IN each one. A line calling out a color that isn't in the shown room reads as
   a visible mistake, not a stylistic choice. Rewrote every entry in
   `opinion_bank.py` to be attitude/philosophy-level instead ("It is never just
   a house") — generic enough to hold up over any of the 50 application photos.
   Apply the same test to any new entries: does this line still make sense over
   literally any of them, not just the one you had in mind while writing it?

2. **Duration was capped** at an arbitrary 12s. Now uses the FULL length of the
   template's audio — an early cutoff mid-track reads as an unfinished edit, not
   a stylistic choice. `compute_segment_boundaries`'s sliver-avoidance logic
   (see above) still applies, just against the real end of the track now
   instead of an artificial one.

3. **Font was DejaVu Sans Bold** — a system fallback, not a considered choice.
   Replaced with Playfair Display (Bold variation of the bundled variable font,
   `hot_takes/fonts/PlayfairDisplay-Bold.ttf` — bundled directly rather than
   relying on it being installed on the GitHub Actions runner, which it isn't
   by default). Matches the editorial/luxury register of Core Decor's own
   swatch-card typography elsewhere in this pipeline, rather than introducing
   an unrelated visual language. PIL's variable-font API needs
   `font.set_variation_by_name("Bold")` explicitly — the file has a weight axis
   from 400-900 and defaults to 400 (regular) if you don't set it.

4. **The boxed backdrop "felt cheap."** Removed entirely. In its place,
   `render_gradient()` in `text_overlay.py` — a soft top-down darkening across
   roughly the top 60% of the frame, fading from ~65% opacity at the very top
   edge to fully transparent, not a banner hugging the text. This is the same
   technique used in high-end real estate and fashion video for exactly this
   legibility problem. Combined with the existing white-fill/black-stroke text
   styling, this held up fine on a real live post against both a bright
   floor-to-ceiling-window kitchen and a warm wood-toned bedroom — two very
   different background tones, same legibility either way.

A note on pacing: a real live run hit a source template with 26 detected cuts
in just 8.1 seconds — averaging roughly 0.3s per segment, much faster than the
first test template's pacing. That's not a bug; different templates genuinely
have different editing rhythms, and this format is deliberately beat-matched to
whatever the day's template actually provides, same philosophy as the main
swatch+application pipeline. Worth knowing about, not necessarily worth
"fixing" unless it turns out to look chaotic rather than energetic in practice —
that's a creative call to revisit with real engagement data, not a code defect.

## Concept asset naming — how a swatch finds its application

`_pair_swatches_with_applications()` matches a swatch to its application shot by
FILENAME PREFIX — everything before the `_swatch` / `_app` suffix must match
exactly. This is the whole pairing mechanism; get the prefix wrong and a pair
silently mismatches (a real bug that already happened once, see "Image pairing").

Convention, four underscore-delimited parts:

```
d01_lib_oxblood_swatch.png   <->   d01_lib_oxblood_app.png
 |    |     |
 |    |     +--- palette/material tag, for humans skimming the folder
 |    +--------- room type: kit, bath, dine, foyer, lib, suite
 +-------------- series letter + zero-padded concept number
```

**Series letter is the load-bearing part for future work.** `c01`-`c50` are the
original set (lighter, warmer neutrals). `d__` is the darker/richer series added
later. Keeping series in separate letter ranges means a new set can never collide
with an existing prefix, and makes it trivial to later have one content type draw
from only one series (e.g. Hot Takes weighted toward the dark set) by filtering on
the first character alone. Room type and palette tag are for legibility only — the
pipeline ignores them.

## Concept asset prep tooling (`concept_tools/`)

Not part of either runtime pipeline — this is asset PREP, run deliberately when
building new concept pairs, never on a schedule. The two helpers below are shared
by both series. `band_swatch.py` and `generate_concept.py` also live in this
folder but belong specifically to the d-series three-band format — see "The
d-series" section below, and note that `generate_concept.py` runs inside GitHub
Actions rather than by hand, for a specific reason documented there.

- `ocr_verify.py` — confirms a freshly generated texture has NO model-rendered
  text before labels are composited. **Uses `--psm 11` and that is load-bearing**:
  tesseract's default PSM 3 returned zero hits on a real swatch card whose three
  material names were plainly legible, a silent false negative that made the check
  worthless. PSM 11 ("sparse text", built for a little text over a busy
  photographic background) caught every word at 91-96% confidence on the same
  image. Validated in BOTH directions — fails a labelled swatch, passes a
  text-free room photo. If this ever reports everything clean, suspect the config
  before believing it.
- `label_swatch.py` — composites the material names using Fry's Baskerville
  (bundled at `concept_tools/fonts/FrysBaskerville.ttf`, sourced as `.woff2` from
  the onlinewebfonts CDN and converted with fontTools+brotli; authenticity
  verified via the embedded name table — Family "Fry's Baskerville", PostScript
  `FrysBaskervilleBT-Roman`, v003.001 — because a filename proves nothing).
  Wide tracking, all caps, NO scrim or background panel (a solid panel reads
  cheap), adaptive ink sampled per line from the actual background luminance
  behind that line, plus one subtle offset shadow. Per-line sampling, not
  per-block: a line straddling mixed light/dark ground can still land marginal,
  which is fine on a uniform card surface but worth knowing.

**Never let the image model render the type.** Flux and similar produce unreliable
spelling and kerning; generate the texture with text explicitly excluded from the
prompt, verify OCR-clean, then label programmatically. This is a standing rule
established after real misrendered output, not a stylistic preference.

## The d-series: three-band concept format — LIVE IN THE REEL ROTATION

**As of 2026-08-14 the d-series is no longer "images only, under test".** d01-d07
were promoted out of `concept_review/` into `assets/swatches` and
`assets/application`, which is the only place the reel pipeline looks. Until then
the entire d-series existed purely as review artefacts and had never appeared in
a published reel. 57 matched pairs now, nothing unmatched on either side.

`concept_offset.txt` was set to 50 — d01's index in the sorted pair list — so the
next reel LEADS with the d-series instead of continuing through the older
c-series.

**A latent bug had to be fixed for this to work at all.** `N_CONCEPTS = 50` was
hardcoded from when the c-series was the whole library, and the concept offset
was taken modulo it. With 57 pairs on disk, indices 50-56 could never be the
START of a reel, so the d-series — and every concept added after it — would have
been reachable only by mid-reel spillover. The count now derives from the actual
asset folders, so rotation covers whatever is really on disk. **If you add
concepts, just drop matched `_swatch`/`_app` pairs into those two folders; no
count needs updating.**

**First d-series reel published 2026-08-14.** 19.8s, 16 concepts, starting
offset 50 — so it opened with all seven d-series concepts (d01-d07) and then ran
on into c01-c09. Instagram media_id 18147586012463215, Facebook video_id
3092586927602898, TikTok 6a7e9cbd6bf062f95aaa15b5, YouTube
6a7e9cc7dcbc3184d7f319fe, template 1/4. Offset advanced 50 -> 9 (50+16 mod 57),
so the NEXT scheduled reel resumes mid-c-series at c10; if the d-series should
lead again, reset `concept_offset.txt` to 50.

**Only APPROVED concepts get promoted.** d08 was deliberately held back — it is
unreviewed and has two open styling questions (an unrequested laptop on the desk;
the leather desk chair and abstract canvas its own styling field names are both
absent).


A parallel concept format being evaluated, **not a replacement for anything
currently running**. The original `c01`-`c50` flat-lay swatch assets and both
runtime pipelines that consume them are untouched and still live. Nothing in this
section is wired into publishing.

**Scope, stated explicitly by Dev and worth not losing**: this is IMAGE
GENERATION ONLY right now. Video stitching and social publishing for this series
come later, as a separate step, once enough concepts are approved. Do not wire it
into any publishing pipeline yet, and do not treat an approved concept as
permission to start.

**The format**, copied in structure from a reference reel Dev supplied: three
full-width horizontal bands of real material TEXTURE — not physical samples
arranged on a flat-lay, which is what the c-series does — each labelled with its
material/colour name in wide-tracked serif caps, ink flipping light or dark per
band. The room shot applies those same three materials 1:1. Pairing is unchanged:
filename prefix, exactly as described in the naming section above.

**Palette direction**: darker, richer, more saturated than the c-series, which
leans light and warm-neutral. That contrast is the entire point of the d-series,
not incidental style drift — don't "correct" a d-series concept back toward the
c-series look.

### Files

- `concept_tools/band_swatch.py` — composes the three-band card. **The bands are
  stacked in CODE from three INDEPENDENTLY generated texture tiles, not generated
  as one image.** Exact horizontal thirds with hard boundaries is precisely the
  geometry image models render inconsistently; stacking programmatically makes it
  exact by construction, and each tile gets a simpler prompt so the texture
  itself comes out better. Same principle as never letting the model render type:
  if code can guarantee it, don't ask the model for it. Imports
  `label_swatch.py`'s font/ink/shadow helpers directly rather than duplicating
  them.
- `concept_tools/generate_concept.py` — BFL FLUX generation of one full concept
  (3 band textures + 1 room shot), OCR-verifying every generated image is
  text-free before any label is composited. Concepts live in a `CONCEPTS` dict in
  this file. Invoked as
  `python concept_tools/generate_concept.py <concept> <out_dir> [all|bands|room]`.
- `.github/workflows/generate-concept.yml` — `workflow_dispatch` ONLY, no
  schedule, taking a `concept` input matching a `CONCEPTS` key and a `parts`
  input. Generation costs real money per image; it must never fire on a timer.
- `concept_tools/edit_room.py` + `.github/workflows/edit-room.yml` — EDITS an
  already-committed room shot in place instead of re-rolling it. See "Editing a
  room instead of re-rolling it" below for when to reach for this rather than
  `parts=room`.

**`parts` (all / bands / room) exists for a real reason** — the two halves of a
concept get approved separately in practice. d01's swatch was approved on its
first pass while its room shot was rejected three times over; regenerating the
whole concept each time would have meant paying for, and risking a re-roll of,
three already-signed-off band textures. The composed swatch card is committed, so
nothing needs the intermediate band textures to rebuild only the room. Reach for
`parts=room` whenever only the room is in question — it is one image instead of
four, and it leaves the approved swatch byte-identical (verified via `git diff`,
not assumed).

### Editing a room instead of re-rolling it — the third axis

`parts=room` re-rolls the WHOLE room shot: camera, architecture, styling, light.
That is right when the room is wrong and wrong when the room is right except for
one fixable flaw, because the good version is gone the moment you re-roll.

d06 forced this. Dev's verdict on its room shot was "I love this application
photo otherwise" — the only problems were two geometry hallucinations. Re-rolling
would have discarded a composition he had just said he liked, gambling on getting
an equally good one back. `edit_room.py` sends the committed image back through
the SAME `flux-2-pro` endpoint with an `input_image` parameter (base64 of the
local file — same auth, same polling, no new model), so only the named thing
changes.

- Invoked as `python concept_tools/edit_room.py <concept> "<instruction>"`, or
  via `edit-room.yml`'s `workflow_dispatch` with a free-text `instruction`.
- **The preservation clause is appended automatically** (`PRESERVE` in that
  module) and must not be dropped. BFL's editing guide is explicit that an edit
  prompt has to state what stays the same as well as what changes; without it an
  edit relights the frame, moves the camera and restyles objects nobody asked
  about, losing the very composition the edit existed to protect.
- Write the instruction the way that guide says: name what changes, refer to
  objects by WHERE THEY ARE in the frame ("the two urns standing on the bottom
  stair tread"), and be specific. Vague directives ("fix the furniture") do not
  work.
- The pre-edit image is kept as a `before-edit-<concept>` workflow artifact, so
  an edit that comes back worse is recoverable. It is stripped before commit.
- **The no-text guard REPORTS on this path but does not gate it**, unlike
  generation — the source was already human-verified text-free, a
  furniture-repositioning edit cannot introduce lettering, and d06's room is the
  confirmed worst case for the guard's false positive. `MIN_CONFIDENCE` is
  untouched and still strict for generation. Do not generalise this exemption
  back into `generate_concept.py`.
- **Known limitation, measured on the first real use:** an edit does not fully
  preserve the identity of the objects it MOVES. d06's edit correctly separated
  the console from the bench, but it also turned one terracotta urn and one blue
  urn into three matching blue ones, and only partly complied on placement —
  moving the urns out of the walking path but leaving them standing on the stair
  treads rather than on the floor as instructed. Expect partial compliance on
  placement and drift on the moved objects specifically; everything untouched
  did hold. Budget for a second pass, and check the result rather than assuming.

### Concept definition shape

Each entry in `CONCEPTS` carries `stem`, `room`, `style`, `styling`, `bands` (3 ×
`{label, texture}`) and `materials_sentence`. Two conventions matter:

1. **`style` and `styling` are per-concept, deliberately not global.** They were
   briefly one shared constant, which would have put the same olive tree and
   landscape painting into every room in the series. Dev asked to keep switching
   decor styles between concepts, and a global object list silently defeats that.
   Only *density* is global (`STYLING_RULE`).
2. **Vary the decor register.** d01 traditional English panelled, d02 warm
   organic modern Mediterranean, d03 restrained Art Deco. Don't let a new concept
   default to the register of the one before it.

### Why generation runs inside GitHub Actions, not locally

`BFL_API_KEY` lives in this repo's Actions secrets, and GitHub's secrets API is
write-only — a value can be set but never read back out, and there is no local
copy of the key anywhere. Rather than have Dev dig up or regenerate a key just to
run something locally, generation runs inside the workflow where the secret is
already usable, and the finished images are committed back to
`concept_review/<concept>/` for review. **This is a deliberate pattern, not a
workaround to undo later** — keep using it for any future BFL generation unless
Dev hands over the key value directly in chat.

### BFL API specifics — learned the hard way, don't rediscover

- Base: `https://api.bfl.ai/v1/flux-2-pro`
- Auth header is `x-key: <key>`, **not** `Authorization: Bearer <key>`.
- `POST` returns `{id, polling_url}`. **Poll the RETURNED `polling_url`**, never
  one you construct yourself — the global endpoint load-balances across clusters,
  so a self-built URL can end up polling the wrong one.
- Poll status values: `Pending` / `Ready` / `Error`.
- On `Ready`, `result.sample` is a URL that **expires in 10 minutes**. Download
  the bytes immediately; never store or reuse the URL itself.
- Width/height should be multiples of 32.
- **The same endpoint also EDITS**: add an `input_image` parameter (an image URL
  or raw base64, no `data:` prefix) and the call becomes an edit of that image
  rather than a fresh generation. No separate model, endpoint or auth. Omit
  width/height when editing so the source's own dimensions carry through.
  Additional references go in `input_image_2` … `input_image_8`.

### BFL prompting rules — from their own docs, checked August 2026

Read before editing any prompt constant. These are documented model behaviours,
not preferences:

- **FLUX.2 does not support negative prompts.** Their words: "focus on describing
  what you want, not what you don't want." Naming a defect can summon it. New
  prompt text must state the DESIRED state instead — `SPATIAL_RULE` is written
  that way deliberately and has no "no ..." clause in it. The older negative
  phrasing in `NO_TEXT`, `BAND_LIGHT` and `ROOM_LIGHT` predates this finding and
  is deliberately left alone: it has five approved concepts behind it, and
  rewriting working prompts to chase a docs quote would be an unvalidated change.
  Don't add NEW negatives, and don't mass-rewrite the old ones without a reason.
- **Word order is weighted** — earlier elements get more attention. Geometry and
  composition go early, which is why `SPATIAL_RULE` sits immediately after
  `COMPOSITION` rather than at the end.
- **Spatial control is done with explicit layering and prepositions** —
  foreground / midground / background, "on", "behind", "in front of", "to the
  right of". This is the documented lever for placement, and the reason the
  d06 edit instruction named objects by where they sit in the frame.
- **Length: their bands are short 10-30, medium 30-80, long 80-300+ words**, with
  the warning "start short, add only what changes the image — more words do not
  automatically mean better results." **The d-series room prompt is now ~533
  words**, well past the top of their long band. That is an OPEN CONCERN, not a
  resolved one: it may be diluting attention across instructions and is a
  plausible contributor to the styling-drift and partial-compliance problems seen
  here. It has NOT been trimmed, because five concepts were approved at roughly
  this length and shortening it is a change worth making deliberately with Dev
  rather than silently. Raise it before adding another constant to that prompt.

Replicate was abandoned for this specific work — that account returned HTTP 402,
insufficient credit — in favour of BFL direct. This doesn't affect anything else
that may still be running on Replicate; check before assuming either way.

### The first real d01 run failed, and why that mattered structurally

Run #1 of `generate-concept.yml` (`workflow_dispatch`, `concept=d01`) failed. It
got bands 1 and 2 generated and OCR-clean, then tripped the no-text check on band
3 (oxblood velvet) with a single hit — `('Yen.', 72.0)` — and exited non-zero.
Three consequences, each worth understanding rather than just retrying past:

1. **The whole concept died on one image.** Bands 1 and 2 had already passed and
   were paid for; both were discarded, and the room shot was never even
   submitted. Failure was all-or-nothing across four independently generated
   images.
2. **The evidence was destroyed.** The offending texture lived only in the
   runner's `concept_review/d01/_textures/`, the workflow uploaded no artifacts,
   and the commit step never ran because it sits after the failing step. So the
   run could report THAT the guard fired but gave no way to judge WHETHER IT
   SHOULD HAVE — and `72.0` is genuinely ambiguous, well below the 91-96% that
   real composited labels scored when `ocr_verify.py` was validated, and exactly
   the kind of score PSM 11 sparse-text mode produces from pile noise on a velvet
   macro.
3. Nothing was committed, so `concept_review/` did not exist at all afterward.

**The fix, and what it deliberately does NOT do**: `_generate_clean()` now
re-rolls the SAME prompt for just the failing image, up to `MAX_TEXT_RETRIES`
(3), instead of failing the concept — generation is stochastic and the prompt
already excludes text, so a hit is usually about that sample rather than that
prompt. Every rejected sample is kept as `<path>.rejected-<n>.png`, and the
workflow uploads them as an artifact on failure (`if: failure()`) so a human can
actually look at what tripped it. They're stripped before the commit step so they
never land in the repo as if they were output.

**The confidence threshold was deliberately left alone.** Relaxing
`MIN_CONFIDENCE` to make one ambiguous hit go away would trade a safeguard that
earned its strictness (see `ocr_verify.py`'s own header) for a single data point.
A prompt that genuinely produces text still fails the concept — it just takes
three samples to establish that instead of one, and now leaves the images behind
to prove it. If a future d-series concept fails here repeatedly, look at the
artifact before touching either the threshold or the prompt.

**The artifact upload is `if: always()`, not `if: failure()`** — and that
distinction was itself a bug found in practice. A run that retries and then
*succeeds* is green, and under `failure()` its rejected samples were deleted
anyway. The very first successful d01 run discarded four of them that way, which
is exactly the evidence-destruction the artifact step existed to prevent, in the
one case nobody had thought to cover.

**Accumulated evidence says the guard fires on texture noise, and that is still
unresolved.** Every hit observed so far is a low-confidence garbage string on
macro texture: `('Yen.', 72.0)`, `('fo,', 63.0)`, `('Vik', 61.0)`, `('Gar', 68.0)`,
`('SSS', 57.0)`, `('EERE', 67.0)`, `('His', 55.0)`, `('ty:', 55.0)`. All sit in a
55-72 band; genuine composited labels scored 91-96 when the module was validated.
One d01 run generated 8 images to deliver 4. The threshold was tuned against a
labelled card and a text-free *room* photo — never against extreme macro texture,
which is the case that misbehaves. **This has been raised with Dev and he has not
ruled on it; do not quietly raise `MIN_CONFIDENCE`.** Note the cost impact and let
him decide.

Separately, room shots routinely contain gibberish lettering on book spines that
OCR passes as clean. Flagged, undecided, arguably fine for a library.

### Room shot lighting — three rejected versions, don't re-litigate

The room half of a d-series concept took four attempts to land. The failures were
all in the PROMPT, never in post-processing, and each one is a trap worth not
re-entering.

- **v1 — "high-contrast directional natural daylight through large windows" plus
  "crisp specular highlights on stone edges, glass and metal."** Produced a hard
  diagonal sun shaft across the panelling and blown highlights. Rejected by Dev as
  "too bright for the mood."
- **v2 — direct sun removed entirely, plus "underexposed roughly one and a half
  stops."** Killed the shaft, but crushed 34.1% of the frame to near-black against
  15-26% in the reference; the sofa and floor lost all detail. Rejected as too
  dark. **Global underexposure is not the lever** — it was never an exposure
  problem.
- **v3 — soft low-angle dawn light, interior practicals turned well up and
  carrying the exposure, shadows explicitly required to hold detail, plus real
  styling.** APPROVED.

There is a measured trap here worth internalising: **v1 was the darkest image of
the entire set by average luminance (57.8) and was still rejected for being too
bright.** The hard shaft read as bright while the frame average was low. Judge
these by the three numbers below, not by impression — eyeballing was wrong twice
in one session, once claiming a velvet colour mismatch that measured as
essentially identical (distance 3.3).

**Measure with mean luminance, blown % (>=250) and crushed % (<=20).** Reference
reel moody rooms sit at mean L 63-71, blown 0.00-0.16%, crushed 15-26%. Approved
d01 landed at 84.5 / 0.06 / 16.8.

Do not reintroduce hard directional daylight, sun shafts, or specular language to
make a room "pop". That exact change has already been rejected once.

### AESTHETIC LIGHTING IS CONTRAST, NOT DARKNESS — read this before touching ROOM_LIGHT

**This is the most-repeated mistake in this project's history. Five prompt
versions and a post-processing tool were all spent chasing the wrong variable.**

v3, v4 and v5 progressively chased DARKNESS — dawn, then late dusk, then "night,
windows dark, no daylight anywhere, most of the frame in deep shadow." Then
`grade_room.py` was built to force the mean-luminance number down with a gamma
curve when the prompt would not. Dev's verdict on that graded result was blunt
and correct: **"very dark and has no lighting at all."**

Both were wrong for the same reason. Aesthetic interior lighting is about the
CONTRAST BETWEEN WARM LIT POOLS AND COOL SHADOW. It is not about how little light
is in the frame. The specifics that actually matter:

- **Warm 2700K interior light against COOL BLUE TWILIGHT at the windows is the
  single defining move.** v5 said the windows were dark with no daylight at all,
  which deleted precisely the contrast that creates the look. Blue hour, not
  night.
- Lamps at **three or four different heights**, each visibly glowing and throwing
  its own pool, overhead light dimmed or out of frame.
- **Shadows tinted cool blue against warm golden highlights** — that colour
  opposition is what reads as "aesthetic" rather than merely dim.
- Texture (bouclé, brass, plaster, stone) catching low raking lamplight.

**A room can be high in average luminance and still look beautifully lit; a dark
room with no visible sources just looks switched off.** Never optimise toward a
target darkness.

**And post-processing cannot create lighting.** A gamma pull dims the lamps along
with everything else, so a flatly-lit frame becomes a flatly-lit dark frame with
less contrast than it started with. `grade_room.py` still exists and its
`measure()` is genuinely useful for reporting mean L / blown / crushed, but
**grading is not the answer to "this doesn't look good", and the numbers are a
diagnostic, not a goal.** The section below records the exposure data honestly;
read it as evidence that darkness was the wrong target, not as a recipe.

**WHAT ACTUALLY WORKED (v6), and the prompt order that goes with it.** Blue hour
just after sunset with every lamp switched on: cool blue twilight in the windows,
warm 2700K practicals layered at three or four heights each visibly glowing and
throwing its own pool with gradual falloff, shadows tinted cool blue, texture
catching low raking light, and an explicit clause that the lamplight reveals the
room's true material colours rather than washing everything amber. d07 came back
exactly right on the first try.

**Prompt ORDER has now been wrong in both directions — know both failure modes:**
- Lighting buried ~400 words in (v3-v5): flat bright daylight, instruction
  effectively ignored.
- Lighting moved to the very front (first v6 run): beautiful light, but the
  concept's materials vanished — d07 returned warm plaster and brass with its
  petrol lacquer, burl walnut and travertine absent, breaking the swatch-to-room
  1:1 match the format exists for.
- **Current, working: MATERIALS first** (stated as the defining feature that must
  be clearly visible), **then ROOM_LIGHT**, then COMPOSITION, then SPATIAL_RULE,
  then styling and fixtures. Both defining properties lead. Don't move either one
  down without re-checking the other.

**And note the number this landed on: mean L 113.0.** That is BRIGHTER than the
graded 77.8 image Dev rejected as "very dark and has no lighting at all", and it
looks incomparably better. Final proof that mean luminance was never the goal.

### Exposure numbers — a diagnostic, and the record of what did not work

Five prompt versions tried to control the room's overall darkness. v1 (hard
daylight) and v2 (blanket underexposure) were rejected on look. v3, v4 and v5
described dawn, then late dusk, then outright night with dark windows and lamps
as the only source — and v5 additionally moved the whole lighting block to the
FRONT of the prompt, where BFL's guide says FLUX weights it most heavily.
Measured on d07, one sample each, against a reference target of mean L 63-71 and
crushed 15-26%:

| version | wording | mean L | crushed % |
|---------|---------|--------|-----------|
| v3 | soft dawn, practicals up | 112.8 | 2.4 |
| v4 | late dusk, practicals dominant | 108.0 | 6.9 |
| v5 | night, dark windows, lamps only, moved to front | **132.6** | 3.3 |

**That is noise, not a trend, and the most extreme wording in the strongest
position came back the brightest of the three.** The model is not disobeying a
weak instruction — it returns the bright editorial interior its training
distribution is saturated with, and a palette of cream boucle, white ceiling and
pale marble pins the histogram bright regardless of the text. Do not "fix" this
by writing a sixth, angrier version of ROOM_LIGHT. That has been tried three
times and costs a paid image per attempt.

`concept_tools/grade_room.py` solves it deterministically: a pure gamma curve on
RGB, exponent bisected to land mean luminance on target. On d07 it took
132.6/3.3% to **77.8 mean L and 24.9% crushed, blown 0.01%** — every number
inside the reference band, first pass, no API call. Gamma is used rather than a
black-point/levels move on purpose: it COMPRESSES shadows instead of clipping
them, so nothing is forced to pure black and shadow detail survives — precisely
the failure that got v2 rejected.

**This is the project's own principle, not a new one.** `band_swatch.py` stacks
bands in code because exact thirds are "what image models render inconsistently",
and labels are composited in code because the model spells unreliably. Same rule:
if code can guarantee it, don't ask the model for it.

**The split of responsibility, which matters if editing either side:**
- The PROMPT owns light QUALITY and DIRECTION — lamps lit, warm, and above all no
  hard sun shafts or blown highlights. Those genuinely cannot be fixed afterwards;
  a baked-in sun shaft stays a sun shaft at any exposure. That is why v1 was a
  prompt failure and had to be fixed as one, and llms.txt's older line that the
  lighting failures were "all in the PROMPT, never in post-processing" remains
  true *for that case*.
- `grade_room.py` owns LEVEL — mean luminance and shadow depth, a global
  monotonic transform, which is the thing post does perfectly and a generative
  model does not.

It also closes the long-standing open finding that room exposure varied with each
palette's own reflectance (d01 84.5 vs d02 111.6 under an identical prompt).
Grading to a target normalises across palettes by construction, so the series can
finally have one consistent mood.

### Styling and composition

Before v3 the room prompt described only architecture — millwork, ceiling coves,
shadow-line baseboards — so the model returned immaculate, completely empty
showrooms. Dev's note was "no photos, no furniture, no decorations." **The model
will not infer furnishing from "luxury interior"; the objects have to be named.**

`STYLING_RULE` governs density only, and is tuned to Dev's words: "not too cramped
and not too empty" — fewer, larger, well-spaced pieces with real breathing room.
Approved d01 sits slightly on the busy side of that target; d02 is closer to it.

`COMPOSITION` uses an eye-level three-quarter view layered front-to-back, replacing
the original dead-centre symmetrical elevation, which read as catalogue
documentation. The reference reel's rooms nearly all place objects in the near
field, and that depth is much of why they look inhabited. True verticals are kept
from the original direction.

### Geometry hallucinations — a THIRD failure axis, separate from light and styling

`SPATIAL_RULE` exists because d06's room shot was committed and presented for
approval with two impossible things in it, and neither lighting nor styling
review would ever have caught them:

1. The console table's rear leg passed straight THROUGH the frame of the rattan
   bench in front of it — two solid objects interpenetrating.
2. Two large urns stood on the bottom stair tread, blocking the only route up.

Dev caught both by eye and circled them; the session that generated it had looked
at the same image and called it good. That is the lesson worth keeping: **a
generative room shot can be correctly lit, correctly styled, correctly materialled
and still be spatially impossible.** The model composes a convincing flat picture
without maintaining a consistent 3D scene underneath it, so solids merge and
circulation routes get furnished over.

`SPATIAL_RULE` states, affirmatively, that the room is a coherent 3D space:
furniture separated by visible floor, legs complete and visible where they meet
the floor, objects back against walls, and doorways, thresholds, stair treads and
the main walking route left open and walkable. It sits right after `COMPOSITION`
so geometry is grouped early in the prompt. It is written with zero negative
clauses on purpose — see the BFL prompting rules above.

**Reviewing a room shot now needs an explicit geometry pass of its own**, separate
from judging mood: trace where each piece of furniture meets the floor, and check
that every walking route and stair is actually passable. Cropping and zooming the
suspect regions is what confirms it — at full-frame scale both d06 defects were
easy to miss and both were obvious once enlarged. Same philosophy as judging
lighting by measured numbers rather than impression.

**`SPATIAL_RULE`'s first real test passed, on all three samples.** d06's room was
re-rolled with `parts=room` after the rule went in. The run tripped the OCR guard
3/3 (again — see below), but all three rejected samples were inspected and every
one of them was geometrically clean: no interpenetrating solids anywhere, and in
the sample that was kept, every stair tread is empty and walkable with the olive
tree's planter and the urn standing on the FLOOR beside the staircase, tucked
against the wall — exactly what the rule asks for, and exactly the defect Dev
sent the previous version back for. Console and foreground stool each show four
legs resting on the floor with open floor between them, verified by zooming in
rather than at full-frame scale.

Three samples is not proof, and the sample size that produced the original defect
was one. Keep doing the geometry pass on new concepts; do not treat this as
solved.

**d07 confirms it is not solved, and shows where the rule is weakest.** d07 was
the first concept generated with `SPATIAL_RULE` in place from the start. Its main
seating group came back clean and verified — the coffee table's pedestal rests
flat with visible floor between it and the sofa's plinth, and the armchair's
chrome legs are grounded and separate. But its FOREGROUND side table is
unresolvable on close inspection: the burl top cantilevers left over the chair's
seat, its left end blending into the chair's burl armrest with no clear boundary,
and its only two legs sit under the right-hand end and reach the floor through
where the chair's base is. At full-frame scale it reads as a normal side table.
Zoomed, it does not resolve.

The pattern across d06 and d07 is worth noting: **the failure has moved to the
near foreground.** `COMPOSITION` deliberately asks for objects in the near field
for depth, and that is where the model has the least room to establish clean
separation. When doing the geometry pass, check the foreground layer FIRST.

**GLOBAL CONSTANTS MUST NOT NAME OBJECTS OR FIXTURES — this mistake has now been
made twice.** The first time, a single global styling constant would have put the
same olive tree and landscape painting into every room; it was moved into
per-concept `styling`. The lighting constant then went on hardcoding *"table lamps
under cream shades"* and *"picture lights above the artwork"* for every room, and
nobody noticed until d05 — a BATHROOM — came back with two table lamps and a
framed picture on the wall that its styling field had never asked for. Dev caught
it by asking, reasonably, why a bathroom had table lamps in it.

`ROOM_LIGHT` now describes light QUALITY only: diffuse, layered, 2700K, arriving
from several heights, shadows holding detail, no sun shafts. Fittings live in each
concept's own `fixtures` field. d05's explicitly rules out table lamps and framed
art on the grounds that it is a wet room. Keep fixture nouns out of the global
constant; there is a check for this worth repeating after edits — assert none of
"table lamp", "picture light", "sconce", "pendant", "downlight", "cove" appears in
`ROOM_LIGHT`.

(For what it's worth, table lamps in a large primary bathroom are a genuine
high-end design move, so the output was not absurd on its face — but it was an
artifact of a global default rather than a decision, and a mains lamp beside a
freestanding tub would fail UK zone regs and US GFCI rules anyway.)

### Band textures must be evenly lit, and labels carry a contrasting halo

Two linked fixes after d04's card shipped with the final letters of CHALK
LIMESTONE completely invisible.

**The halo.** Adaptive ink picks one colour per line from the MEAN luminance
behind it. That band contained near-black blotches, so the mean said "light
ground, use dark ink" while part of the word sat over near-black. A stronger drop
shadow cannot fix this — the shadow is always black, so under dark ink over a dark
patch it adds nothing. `label_swatch.draw_label()` now draws a soft blurred
contour in the CONTRASTING tone: dark behind pale ink, pale behind dark ink. It is
invisible on an even texture and only does work where the ground fights the ink,
so the module's no-scrim rule still holds.

**`BAND_LIGHT`.** The band prompt used to ask for "subtle low-angle raking light"
and a "deep, rich, saturated, moody dark colour grade". Raking light bakes
vignettes and hot stripes into a tile that is then used as a TYPOGRAPHIC
BACKGROUND, which is what created the blotches. It also darkened tiles below the
same material in the room shot. Band textures are now flat, even and shadowless,
which both fixed the legibility and moved the cards closer to the reference reel's
own flat, calm cards.

**`concept_tools/check_legibility.py` is the metric, and MEASURE PER GLYPH.**
Compare a character's own pixels against the ring immediately around it. A line or
column average mixes glyph, halo and background together: it hid this failure
completely and separately invented a fake one, wrongly flagging AGED ELM at 43.1
on a card where the correct metric scores it 102.7. On the broken d04 card the
final E of LIMESTONE scored 0.9 out of 255; after both fixes it scores 122.4, and
all fifteen labels across d01-d05 pass with a worst case of 67.8. The script exits
non-zero on any character below 45, so it can gate a run.

### Room exposure depends on the concept's own palette

An open finding, not yet acted on. d01 and d02 use an identical lighting prompt
and landed 27 points apart — d01 at mean L 84.5, d02 at 111.6 with crushed shadows
collapsing to 2.6%. The cause is the palette's own reflectance: d01's near-black
marble and fumed oak absorb light where d02's travertine floor and cream plaster
bounce it. So a fixed lighting instruction yields systematically brighter rooms
for lighter concepts. If the series ever needs consistent mood across concepts,
the lighting spec has to become palette-aware rather than fixed. Dev approved d02
as generated with this known.

Related, also raised and consciously left alone: d02's band textures carry heavy
baked-in lighting gradients (the walnut is nearly black at its edges, the
travertine has a hot stripe through the middle), which loosens the swatch-to-room
material match — walnut and travertine drifted 71 and 79 in RGB distance against
olive limewash's 14. The band prompt still asks for "subtle low-angle raking
light" and a "moody dark colour grade", which fights the flat, evenly-lit look the
reference cards actually have. Fixable via `parts=bands` without touching an
approved room shot.

## Hosting

Reels are committed straight into this repo's own `media/reels/` and served via
`raw.githubusercontent.com` — the same free pattern already running in the
`millionchallenge` repo. `upload_video_to_public_host()` auto-prunes to the 10 most
recent reels each run. No paid storage, no new secret required in GitHub Actions
(the checkout step already leaves the workflow authenticated to push).

## TikTok and YouTube publishing via Buffer

`publish_to_buffer()` handles both. Direct-API integration for TikTok (app review)
and YouTube (OAuth verification for unverified apps) was judged too high-friction
for what this needs, so Buffer's GraphQL API (`api.buffer.com/graphql`) is used
instead, on a personal API key (Free plan) — not the old OAuth-app path, which is
closed to new developers and isn't what this uses.

This lives on a **separate, dedicated Buffer account**
(`devkumardave26@gmail.com`), deliberately not the account `the_higher_being`'s
pipeline uses. That account is already at 4 channels (Threads/Pinterest/X, paid
plan) — over the Free tier's hard 3-channel cap. Mixing Core Decor in there would
mean paying for capacity Core Decor doesn't need. This account has exactly 2 of 3
free channel slots used (TikTok `abz_dev`, YouTube "Core Decor") — one spare.

Mechanically: `createPost` mutation, video as `{"video": {"url": ...}}` pointing at
the same `raw.githubusercontent.com` URL already used for Meta, `mode: shareNow`,
`schedulingType: automatic`. YouTube additionally requires `title` (in both the
asset's own `metadata` AND the top-level `metadata.youtube` block — both are
needed, confirmed by testing, not assumed) and `categoryId` (hardcoded to `"26"`,
Howto & Style — revisit if that stops fitting the content) — TikTok needs neither.
Enum values are lowercase (`public`, not `PUBLIC` — this rejected on the first real
test, GraphQL's own error names the correct value).

Tested against real posts on both platforms — actual `sent` status confirmed via a
follow-up query, not just trusting the mutation's immediate response — before this
was wired into the daily pipeline.

**Known tradeoff, not a bug**: identical content goes to all four platforms. Fast
to stand up, not platform-native — TikTok and YouTube Shorts each have their own
conventions (trending sounds, punchier titles) that this doesn't yet account for.

## Odd-segment fix history — three versions, read this before touching it again

`build_reel()` needs an even number of segments (so the reel always ends on an
application shot, never a swatch). When a template's raw cut count is odd, one
extra thing has to happen to force it even. This has been through three real
versions — know why the first two weren't good enough before "simplifying" back
to either of them.

**v1 — always drop the first internal boundary.** Simple, but meant always
sacrificing the opening beat. Confirmed on a real published post (`Dbqgm1IjR4c`):
a template with cuts at `[1.73, 4.0, 5.73, 7.73, 9.73, 11.97, 13.8, 15.77]` (9
segments, odd) had its 1.73s opening beat silently merged into a flat 4.0s
opening hold — "first frame holds too long, missing a beat," caught by eye, not
by any test, since the code was doing exactly what it was told to do.

**v2 — drop whichever boundary produces the smallest merged segment**, instead of
always the first. Fixed the opening-beat problem on that specific template (the
merge moved to the middle instead). But confirmed broken again on a DIFFERENT real
post, a different template (`Reel_template_3.mp4`, cuts at `[2,4,6,8,10,12]`,
14.09s duration) — every segment there is close to uniform length, so "smallest
merge" has no better option to pick; it's forced to double whichever pair it
lands on regardless. Merging two similar-sized things always produces something
roughly twice as big — that's the actual structural limit of merging at all, not
a bug in the "which one to merge" heuristic.

**v3 — current — split instead of merge.** Never drop a boundary; instead pick
the LONGEST existing segment and cut it into two equal halves that both show the
SAME image (a genuine cut event, content doesn't change, but going from odd to
even by ADDING a boundary rather than removing one). This means every original
template timestamp survives untouched, always — verified by rebuilding both real
templates that broke v1 and v2 and confirming, via direct ffmpeg scene-detection
on the actual output file, that 100% of original cuts are present in both cases.

**Known, accepted side effect of v3, not a bug**: the split itself is often
visually and algorithmically invisible — cutting from a static image to an
identical copy of itself produces zero pixel change, so scene detection (and a
human eye) won't register it as a cut at all. This is fine: the split always
lands on the segment with the most slack (typically a template's own deliberate
slow ending, or trailing leftover duration past the last real cut) — exactly the
place where an invisible extra cut costs nothing, because there was no tight beat
being protected there in the first place. The alternative (v1/v2's merge) always
had a VISIBLE cost wherever it landed; v3's cost is real but consistently
imperceptible. That tradeoff is why v3 replaced v2 outright rather than sitting
alongside it as an option.

**Implementation detail that matters if touching this again**: `segments` is a
list of `(start, end, source_index)`, not just `(start, end)`. The split
duplicates one `source_index` across two segments — pair-advancement logic must
check `src != prev_src` (not list position) before advancing, or a split would
wrongly advance the pair between two segments that should show the same image.
It must also compare against `last_original_src` by identity, not against "last
position in the list" — if the split happens to land on the segment that was
originally last, position-based checks break (the true final application no
longer occupies "the last position" alone; both its halves need to NOT trigger a
pair advance between them, checking by src makes this correct in either case).

If a future post still looks like it's missing a beat or out of sync with its
source template, the diagnostic process that found both prior bugs generalizes:
run ffmpeg scene-detection on both the source template and the actual delivered
output, list both sets of cut timestamps, and diff them directly. Don't reason
about it in the abstract — the exact numbers are what caught both real bugs.

**A fourth, smaller issue found the same way**: comparing full-precision (not
rounded-for-display) timestamps between a source template and a rebuild showed 6
of 8 cuts landing frame-exact, but the 6th and 7th each drifted by exactly one
frame (+0.033s) — not random noise, and never a whole second, but a consistent
one-frame overshoot appearing only on later cuts. Cause: durations were computed
from unsnapped boundaries, and each clip's frame count got rounded independently
when rendered — tiny sub-frame error compounding across the sequence until it
tipped over a full frame several cuts in. Fixed by snapping every boundary to an
exact frame multiple (`round(t * FPS) / FPS`) BEFORE computing any duration, not
after — the same technique already used in the separate algorithmic beat-sync
function elsewhere in this file, which just never got applied to this path.
Verified frame-exact (zero drift on all 8 cuts, not just most) after the fix.

## Missed-run recovery

The 14:00 UTC daily-reel run can fail silently in ways that aren't a code bug at
all — confirmed once: a run's job-level conclusion came back "cancelled" with an
empty step log and no retrievable log blob, while the run-level conclusion said
"failure" — a GitHub Actions infrastructure hiccup, not anything in this pipeline.
With no automatic recovery, that meant a full day with no post and nobody finding
out until asked about it directly.

`missed-post-check.yml` runs at 20:00 UTC (6 hours of margin — enough that a run
which is just taking a while doesn't get mistaken for one that failed), queries the
Actions API for whether daily-reel.yml has a successful run today, and triggers one
itself via `workflow_dispatch` if not. Mirrors the same pattern already proven out
on the `millionchallenge`/`the_higher_being` pipelines (`token-expiry-check.yml`,
`missed-post-check.yml` there) — this wasn't invented fresh, it's applying a
pattern that already works elsewhere in Dev's other projects.

This covers *silent scheduling/infra failures specifically*. It does not mean every
possible failure mode is now unattended-proof — a genuine code regression (like the
Facebook truncation bug once was) still needs a real fix, not just a retry; retrying
a broken pipeline just fails again. Check *why* a recovery run was needed before
assuming a retry alone was the right answer.

## Secrets (names only — see SECRETS_SETUP.md, never put values in any file)

`META_SYSTEM_USER_TOKEN` (actually a personally-derived long-lived Page token as of
the Facebook publishing fix above — see that section before regenerating this),
`META_IG_BUSINESS_ACCOUNT_ID`, `META_PAGE_ID`, `GOOGLE_OAUTH_CLIENT_ID`,
`GOOGLE_OAUTH_CLIENT_SECRET`, `GOOGLE_OAUTH_REFRESH_TOKEN` (for pulling templates
from Drive — read from env by drive_upload.py, not a local file, so this works
unattended in Actions), `BUFFER_API_KEY` (personal key on the dedicated Core Decor
Buffer account, see the Buffer section above — NOT the_higher_being's account),
`BUFFER_TIKTOK_CHANNEL_ID`, `BUFFER_YOUTUBE_CHANNEL_ID`, `BFL_API_KEY` (BFL FLUX
image generation for the d-series — used only by `generate-concept.yml`, by
neither runtime pipeline; see the d-series section for why generation runs inside
Actions rather than locally). `SWATCH_ASSETS_DIR`/
`APPLICATION_ASSETS_DIR` are workflow-set paths into this repo's own assets/
folder, not secrets. `META_APP_ID` and `GDRIVE_INPUT_PATH` are no longer used — the
Reels API doesn't need an app ID, and input now comes from the Drive Template Reels
rotation, not a watched local folder.

## Giving a new AI agent access to this repo

A new AI session needs different things depending on what it's being asked to do.
Work out which of these applies before asking Dev for anything.

**Just reading/understanding the project** — needs nothing. This repo is public;
any AI with a `git clone`, a `web_fetch`-style tool, or GitHub's own web UI can read
everything including this file without any credential at all.

**Editing code and pushing commits, or managing GitHub Actions secrets** — needs a
GitHub Personal Access Token, created fresh for the session, not reused across
sessions:
- Dev generates one at https://github.com/settings/personal-access-tokens/new
- Fine-grained, scoped to **only this repo** (`devdave666/core-decor-automation`),
  not all repos
- Permissions needed: **Contents** (Read and write), **Actions** (Read and write —
  needed both for triggering `workflow_dispatch` runs and for managing the
  encrypted secrets store)
- This is deliberately session-only — ask Dev for a fresh one rather than assuming
  a token from a prior conversation still works; there's no reason to keep a
  long-lived PAT sitting around for a repo this size.
- To actually SET secret values (not just know their names), the encryption step
  needs `PyNaCl` — GitHub's secrets API requires the value be sealed with the
  repo's own public key first, plain PUT requests with a raw value will fail.

**Testing/debugging against the real live platforms directly (not through GitHub
Actions)** — e.g. running `publish_to_facebook()` or `publish_to_buffer()` by hand
to isolate a bug, the way most of the debugging in this project actually happened —
needs the actual secret VALUES, not just names. GitHub's secrets API is write-only;
a token can set a secret but can never read one back. So for this, Dev needs to
paste the actual current value of whatever secret is relevant (Meta Page token,
Buffer API key, etc.) directly into the conversation. Verify any pasted credential
actually works (a cheap read-only API call, like `debug_token` for Meta or an
`account { id }` query for Buffer) before trusting it or using it for anything
real — this project's history is full of credentials that looked right and weren't.

**Publishing an actual real post** as part of debugging (not just checking status)
means real, live content going out on real accounts — treat this the same caution
as a production deploy, not a throwaway test. Mark test posts as such in the
caption so they're identifiable for cleanup, and don't delete live posts across any
of these platforms without Dev doing it himself — that boundary held throughout
this project's history and should keep holding for future sessions too.

## Open / unresolved as of this writing

- The long-lived Page token backing `META_SYSTEM_USER_TOKEN` depends on the
  underlying personal Facebook account's login staying valid — no fixed expiry, but
  a password change would invalidate it. If that becomes a real problem, Business
  Verification is the alternative (see the Facebook publishing section above for why
  it was skipped initially).
- The exact mechanism behind the concatenation-triggers-truncation bug on the
  general Video API (documented in detail above) was never confirmed at the Meta-
  infrastructure level — only that switching to the Reels API entirely avoids it.
  If a future change ever needs the general `/videos` endpoint again for non-Reels
  content, do not assume this is fixed there; re-test.
- Posting time (currently 14:00 UTC, in the workflow's cron schedule) is a
  placeholder, not a researched choice — worth revisiting once there's enough
  engagement data to know what actually performs better.
- Content is identical across all four platforms — not yet platform-native (see
  the Buffer section above for the specific tradeoff).
- The TikTok handle connected (`abz_dev`) was flagged once as possibly not the
  intended dedicated Core Decor account, worth Dev double-checking if that hasn't
  happened yet.
- `missed-post-check.yml` is new and has not yet actually had to recover a real
  missed run since being added — the query logic was verified against real
  historical data before shipping, but its first live trigger (if/when one happens)
  is still worth confirming actually worked end-to-end.
- **d-series band/room timing rhythm — genuinely undecided, ask before assuming.**
  The reference video holds its swatch band for ~0.7s and the room shot for ~1.0s
  (swatch deliberately shorter than the payoff), while the existing runtime
  pipeline gives both beats equal weight from template timing. Whether the
  d-series should adopt that uneven rhythm was still mid-conversation when the
  pivot to "images first, video later" happened, and was never settled. Don't
  default to either answer when video stitching for this series actually starts —
  raise it with Dev.
- **The d-series remains images-only.** Nothing about it is connected to
  publishing, and no video stitching exists for it. Dev reviews each concept by
  eye before the next is generated — generate one at a time, not a batch. Status:

  | id | room | style | bands | status |
  |----|------|-------|-------|--------|
  | d01 | library | traditional English panelled | Nero Marquina / Fumed Oak / Oxblood Velvet | APPROVED |
  | d02 | dining | warm organic modern Mediterranean | Olive Limewash / European Walnut / Travertine | APPROVED |
  | d03 | suite | restrained Art Deco | Aubergine Lacquer / Antique Brass / Alabaster | APPROVED |
  | d04 | kitchen | Belgian minimalist wabi-sabi | Indigo Limewash / Aged Elm / Chalk Limestone | APPROVED |
  | d05 | bathroom | Japandi | Teal Tadelakt / Charred Cedar / Pale Hinoki | APPROVED |
  | d06 | foyer | Moroccan riad eclectic | Cobalt Zellige / Hammered Brass / Sand Limewash | APPROVED |
  | d07 | living | Italian postwar modernist (Milanese) | Petrol Lacquer / Burl Walnut / Roman Travertine | APPROVED — first concept lit by ROOM_LIGHT v6 |
  | d08 | study | Brutalist / raw-material modernism | Board-Formed Concrete / Patinated Bronze / Oatmeal Wool | awaiting review — lighting and geometry clean; laptop and missing desk chair queried |
  | d09 | living | transitional American classic | Navy Panelling / Cognac Leather / Ivory Linen | generating — built from a reference Dev supplied |

  All six room types from the original naming convention (`kit`, `bath`, `dine`,
  `foyer`, `lib`, `suite`) were in use as of d06, so d07 onward introduces NEW
  room-type tags. That is fine and expected — the pipeline ignores the room tag
  entirely, it exists for humans skimming the folder. Keep them short and
  obvious, and keep the series letter + number as the load-bearing part.
  **Dev's standing palette steer as of d04: bluer tones with textured paint**, and
  keep switching decor register between concepts.

  **d09 is the first concept built from a REFERENCE Dev supplied rather than from
  a style brief** — an Instagram post (@styledandorganizedhome, "7 color
  combinations that always work") at 7.2k likes and 4.1k shares. A share count
  that high relative to likes is reach-driving behaviour, so treat that palette
  (navy panelling / cognac leather / ivory linen, warm brass, black marble) as
  validated by real engagement rather than guessed. This is the same logic that
  created Hot Takes: when real numbers point somewhere, follow them. It also puts
  blue back after d08 deliberately broke the run.

  **d06's room shot needed a manual override — read before assuming `parts=all`
  always self-recovers.** Two straight `parts=all` runs both failed: bands passed
  OCR-clean every time, but the room shot tripped the no-text guard 3/3 attempts
  in each run (6 rejects total, every hit 55-64% confidence). This is the same
  "guard fires on noise" pattern below, but the first confirmed instance where the
  noise source was an ORNATE PATTERN (the zellige tile mosaic and stair ironwork)
  rather than macro texture — worth knowing the false-positive isn't texture-only.
  Since both runs die before the commit step, all 3 clean band textures from each
  attempt were thrown away too, not just the room. Fix applied: downloaded the
  failed run's `rejected-d06` artifact, inspected all 3 rejected room images by
  eye (none contained real text), rejected one for an unrelated styling-drift bug
  (a framed photo on the console the concept never asked for — same class of
  mistake as d05's table lamps), then manually ran the sample that best matched
  `CONCEPTS["d06"]["styling"]` through `_fit_final` and committed it directly —
  bypassing the automated guard for this one image, not by relaxing
  `MIN_CONFIDENCE`. A separate cheap `parts=bands` run recovered the swatch card.
  If a future concept dies the same way, this is the recovery path: pull the
  artifact, eyeball the rejects, hand-place the best one rather than blindly
  re-running `parts=all` a third time and re-paying for bands that already passed.
- **The OCR guard's `MIN_CONFIDENCE` was RAISED 55 -> 85 by Dev on 2026-08-14**,
  after every hit across all nine concepts turned out to be a false positive in
  a 55-83 band while real composited labels scored 91-96. There has never been
  a true positive above 83. The cost of 55 was real: d06's room never passed
