  once in nine attempts, and d09 lost a whole concept — two already-paid,
  already-passing bands discarded — to ('wake', 60.0) on a linen weave.
  The standing rule that the model must never render type is UNCHANGED: the
  prompt still excludes text, the guard still runs on every image, and genuine
  legible words score far above 85. **Still to confirm on the next Actions run:
  the both-directions validation (a labelled card must still FAIL) has not been
  re-run at 85 — pytesseract is not installed locally.** If a real rendered word
  ever slips through below 85, lower it again and record the sample.
- Room exposure varies with each concept's own palette reflectance under an
  identical lighting prompt — 84.5 (d01) vs 111.6 (d02) mean luminance. Only
  matters if consistent mood across the series becomes a requirement.
- Swatch-to-room material drift, the most persistent issue in the series, now has
  a working method. **Compare HUE AND SATURATION SEPARATELY — raw RGB distance is
  the wrong metric** and is what made this look unfixable for six concepts. Since
  ROOM_LIGHT v6 the room is deliberately lamplit while `BAND_LIGHT` keeps the
  bands flat and evenly lit for label legibility, so every material measures
  darker in the room than on its tile, and raw RGB distance mostly reports that
  lighting difference rather than any real mismatch. On d07 raw distance said all
  three bands drifted (63 / 27 / 37); split apart, hue was already correct on all
  three and only saturation was off.
  Worked example, d07 retuned via `parts=bands` against the approved room:
  walnut went from S=95 (fiery orange-red) against the room's 63, to within 17;
  travertine from S=1 (dead neutral grey) against the room's 20, to within 12;
  hue within 1-5 degrees on all three. The travertine was also renamed from
  "Silver Travertine" to "Roman Travertine" because the approved room shows warm
  cream stone, not silver — **check the band NAME against the room too, not just
  its colour.**
  A tile will never match a moody room on BRIGHTNESS and should not be made to;
  `BAND_LIGHT` stays flat. Hue and saturation are the things that can match.
  Historical raw-distance figures, kept for context but not comparable to the
  above: d02 walnut 71 and travertine 79, d03 alabaster 77, d02 limewash 14.
- Room shots contain gibberish lettering on book spines that OCR passes as clean.
  Flagged, undecided.
- **The d-series room prompt is ~533 words, well past BFL's own recommended
  ceiling** (their "long" band tops out around 300, with an explicit warning that
  more words do not mean better results). Untouched because five concepts were
  approved at roughly this length, but it is a plausible contributor to styling
  drift and to instructions being only partly obeyed. Raise with Dev before
  adding anything further to that prompt.
- **d06's room shot was re-rolled rather than edited further, at Dev's call.** The
  edited version fixed the console-through-bench intersection but only partly
  complied on the urns (off the walkway, still on the treads) and restyled them
  in the process. The re-roll under `SPATIAL_RULE` came back clean on all three
  samples and is what is committed. The edited version is not lost — it is in
  git history at `a494b11`, recoverable with
  `git checkout a494b11 -- concept_review/d06/d06_foyer_cobalt_app.png`.
- **d06 has now tripped the OCR no-text guard 9 times out of 9 room-shot
  attempts**, across three separate runs (two `parts=all`, one `parts=room`),
  every hit low-confidence garbage on zellige tile and stair ironwork. Its room
  shot has never once passed the guard, and every committed version of it has
  been placed by hand after visual inspection. This is the strongest single piece
  of evidence yet that `MIN_CONFIDENCE` is miscalibrated for ornate pattern.
  Still not changed unilaterally — but d06 is the concept to point at when
  deciding.

## Single Product Reel — the third content type (2026-08-14)

Added `single_product_reel/single_product_pipeline.py` and
`.github/workflows/single-product-reel.yml` for a format neither the original
swatch+application rotation (`core_decor_reel_pipeline.py`) nor Hot Takes
(`hot_takes/`) cover: a ONE-OFF product drop from a Drive folder Dev points it
at, containing exactly one swatch photo and any number of application photos
of that same product — not the committed `assets/` pool, not a paired
swatch/application filename convention.

Built the same way Hot Takes was built alongside the original pipeline: reuses
every shared stage (Drive fetching, audio mastering, template cut-timing
extraction, Meta/Buffer publishing, repo hosting, the git-backed counter
helper) directly from `core_decor_reel_pipeline.py`, with its own
`single_product_reel/template_index.txt` so its position in the Drive Template
Reels rotation never collides with the other two pipelines' counters — same
reasoning already recorded above for Hot Takes' own `_fetch_template_for_audio`.

**Reel structure**: segment 0 is always the swatch (the anticipation beat),
every later segment is `random.choice(application_photos)` chosen WITH
replacement — repeats across segments are expected and correct, not a bug, per
Dev's literal instruction ("cycle through all the applications randomly even
they repeat"). Because the swatch only ever appears in segment 0, the reel is
guaranteed to end on an application shot for any template with 2+ cuts, with
none of `core.build_reel`'s parity/alternation bookkeeping needed — that
bookkeeping exists there specifically to keep a fixed swatch/application PAIR
alternating correctly, which doesn't apply here.

**Swatch detection**: whichever file in the folder has `"swatch"` in its name
(case-insensitive). If none match, falls back to the first file alphabetically
and logs a warning — worth checking on the first run of a new folder that
doesn't follow this naming convention, since a silent wrong guess here would
mean an application photo gets used as the opening "material" shot instead of
the actual swatch.

**Product name**: `PRODUCT_NAME` workflow input if given, otherwise the Drive
folder's own display name via the new `drive_upload.get_folder_name()`. Rename
the Drive folder to something caption-worthy before dispatching if the raw
folder name wouldn't read well in a caption.

**"A song already in our library"**: resolved with Dev as meaning the next
Template Reel in the existing Drive Template Reels rotation — its mastered
audio AND its real cut-timing, exactly the mechanism the other two pipelines
already use. There is no separate music library in this repo; every track this
project has ever posted with came from that same folder.

**Captions, per Dev's instruction, deliberately two different shapes** — see
the new functions in `caption_bank.py`:
  - `get_link_in_bio_caption(product_name)` → Instagram, Facebook, TikTok,
    YouTube. Short hook + a natural link-in-bio CTA naming the product, same
    "don't read as AI-written" voice as `get_caption()` but no rotation index
    (this is a one-off run, not a pool to cycle through without repeats).
  - `get_pinterest_seo_caption(product_name)` → Pinterest only. Deliberately
    long and keyword-front-loaded, not just a longer version of the other
    caption — Pinterest's own search surfaces reward descriptive, keyword-dense
    pin text, and front-load the product name + keywords since Pinterest
    truncates descriptions in search results.

**Pinterest publishes via Buffer** (`core.publish_to_buffer(..., platform=
"pinterest")`) — Dev confirmed Pinterest is already a connected Buffer channel,
referenced as the new `BUFFER_PINTEREST_CHANNEL_ID` secret, same as the
existing `BUFFER_TIKTOK_CHANNEL_ID` / `BUFFER_YOUTUBE_CHANNEL_ID` pattern.
Deliberately uses `publish_to_buffer`'s plain minimal path — caption text + one
video asset, no extra `metadata` block — rather than guessing at a
title/board field the way the YouTube branch does for `categoryId`/`privacy`.
Buffer's exact GraphQL input schema for Pinterest posts (title separate from
description? board selection, or does the channel already imply one board?)
has never been tested against this project's real Buffer account. Dev's own
words: "it's okay if you can't write a custom caption for it, I can probably
update it later" — so the first real run through this workflow IS the test;
if Buffer rejects or mishandles the Pinterest post, add the missing metadata
field to the `if platform == "pinterest":` branch of `publish_to_buffer()`
afterward, the same way the YouTube branch was built, rather than guessing now.

This workflow is `workflow_dispatch` only, no schedule — same "deliberate act"
reasoning as `generate-concept.yml`: it corresponds to one specific Drive
folder Dev has just pointed it at, not a recurring rotation.

## Carousel Post — the fourth content type (2026-08-17, multi-concept 2026-08-18)

Added `carousel_post/carousel_pipeline.py`, `carousel_post/prepare_image.py`
and `.github/workflows/carousel-post.yml` for a format none of the first
three content types cover: a static multi-IMAGE carousel, not a video. Each
post cycles through `CONCEPTS_PER_CAROUSEL` (4) c-series concepts, and each
concept contributes its own swatch-then-application pair in order — the
same "swatch is the anticipation beat, application is the payoff" reveal
logic already used throughout the video reel pipelines, repeated per concept
across the carousel instead of a single pair. No audio, no cut-timing, no
ffmpeg, no librosa at all. First content type in the repo that needs none of
them.

**Originally shipped as ONE concept per post (2 images).** Dev's instruction
2026-08-18: a carousel should be multiple slides showing more than one
concept, not just one swatch+application pair. `run_pipeline()` now reads
`CONCEPT_INDEX_FILE` as a START index, takes `CONCEPTS_PER_CAROUSEL`
consecutive concepts (wrapping via modulo, same as before), and advances the
counter by however many concepts were actually used — not by 1 — so the
rotation still covers every concept exactly once per full cycle regardless of
batch size. 4 concepts = 8 images per post, safely under Instagram's 10-child
carousel limit. `publish_carousel_to_instagram` already took an arbitrary-
length `image_urls` list (no code change needed there beyond a docstring
update) — the 2-image assumption only lived in the caller.

**Scope is deliberately the ORIGINAL c-series only (c01-c50)**, filtered out
of the same `assets/swatches` / `assets/application` folders the d-series now
also lives in — `carousel_pipeline._c_series_pairs()` reuses
`core._pair_swatches_with_applications()` then keeps only stems starting with
`"c"`. Dev asked for this against the c-series specifically; nothing stops a
d-series carousel from being a later, separate decision the way d-series
video publishing will be.

**Own counters**, both under `carousel_post/`: `concept_index.txt` and
`caption_index.txt`. Same reasoning already recorded above for Hot Takes —
reusing the root-level `concept_offset.txt`/`caption_index.txt` would race
this pipeline's position against the main daily pipeline's whenever both run
close together. `caption_index.txt` here is a plain unbounded increment (no
modulo applied before writing), matching how the main pipeline's own
`advance_caption_index` behaves — `caption_bank.get_caption()` already mods
everything it needs internally.

### The JPEG + aspect-ratio problem — READ THIS, the approach changed once already

This project's swatch/application assets are 1072x1920 (9:16, ratio 0.5625) —
built for the video reels. Two real constraints, confirmed against Meta's own
current docs before writing any code (not assumed): the content-publishing
API accepts **JPEG only** — a PNG `image_url` is rejected outright — and feed/
carousel images must fall within a **4:5 to 1.91:1** aspect ratio. 9:16 is far
outside that band on both counts.

**v1 — fit-inside + blurred pillarbox — shipped, posted for real, then
rejected on the actual live result.** Since 4:5 (0.8) is proportionally WIDER
per unit height than 9:16 (0.5625), the reasoning was: fit the WHOLE source
inside a 4:5 canvas by shrinking to the HEIGHT, and fill the empty left/right
space with a blurred, darkened extension of the same image (the technique
Instagram's own app uses when a taller photo is posted to feed) — content-
preserving by construction, nothing ever cropped. It worked exactly as
designed and still looked wrong: Dev's verdict on the first real post was
that the blurred side bars just read as empty space, not a considered design
choice. **Content preservation was optimized for at the expense of the actual
visual result — worth remembering before re-deriving "never crop, only pad"
as obviously correct on the next image-shape problem.**

**v2 — current — full-bleed COVER crop, anchored to protect the swatch
label.** Dev's instruction after seeing v1 live: losing some top/bottom is
fine, as long as the swatch card's material-name text stays visible. Scale
the source to COVER the 4:5 canvas completely (width is always the binding
dimension for this project's 9:16-into-4:5 case, so overflow is always in
HEIGHT) and crop the overflow — `prepare_carousel_image(src, dest, anchor_y)`
in `prepare_image.py`, where `anchor_y` places the crop window vertically
(0.0 keeps the top, 1.0 keeps the bottom, 0.5 is centered). `carousel_
pipeline.py` calls it with **anchor_y=1.0 for the swatch** — crop only ever
comes off the TOP, so the label (bottom fifth of frame on c01) survives
regardless of exactly where it sits on any given concept — and **anchor_y=0.5
for the application shot**, a normal centered crop, since it has no
text-survival constraint. Verified by eye against c01's real assets after the
change: full-bleed on both images, no side bars, and the swatch label sits
comfortably inside the frame with margin to spare.

### Publishing shape is genuinely different per platform, not just "post the image"

Added to `core_decor_reel_pipeline.py` rather than inside `carousel_post/`,
since these lean on the exact same `_graph_post`/`_graph_get`/`PipelineError`
plumbing already centralized there — genuinely shared, not content-type-
specific, same bar as everything else that lives in that file rather than a
subfolder.

- **Instagram** (`publish_carousel_to_instagram`) — a different container
  SHAPE from the REELS path, not a variant of it: each image becomes its own
  `is_carousel_item` child container first, then one parent container with
  `media_type=CAROUSEL` and `children` referencing all child ids gets
  published. Order is preserved exactly as passed in.
- **Facebook** (`publish_photo_post_to_facebook`) — Facebook Pages have no
  carousel object at all. The equivalent is an ordinary `/feed` post with
  multiple photos attached: upload each photo UNPUBLISHED first
  (`published=false` to `/{page_id}/photos`) so it doesn't appear as its own
  standalone post, then one `/feed` post with `attached_media` referencing all
  the resulting photo ids. Facebook's own UI renders this as a swipeable
  gallery.
- **TikTok / Pinterest** (`publish_image_carousel_to_buffer`) — best-effort,
  attempted via Buffer, same as everything else this project reaches through
  Buffer rather than a direct API. **UNVERIFIED against this project's real
  Buffer account as of when this was written** — same "first real run is the
  test" position already taken for the Pinterest video path in
  `single_product_reel` (see that section above). The asset shape
  (`{"image": {"url": ...}}` per entry, ordered list for multiple images) is
  confirmed from Buffer's own current API docs, not guessed — what's NOT
  confirmed is whether Buffer actually surfaces multiple image assets as a
  real swipeable carousel on TikTok's "photo mode" or a Pinterest multi-image
  pin for THIS project's connected channels, versus posting only the first
  image, or rejecting multi-image assets outright for a given channel type.
  **A failure here does not fail the run** — `carousel_pipeline.run_pipeline()`
  wraps both calls in try/except and only logs a warning, since IG and FB are
  the proven, required platforms for this format and shouldn't be blocked by
  an unverified extra path. If either misbehaves on a real run, check the
  actual response body before assuming the schema is wrong.
- **YouTube — not attempted at all**, unlike TikTok/Pinterest. This project's
  YouTube channel is wired via Buffer for Shorts VIDEO content only, and there
  is no image/carousel post surface available through that same channel. This
  isn't "untested", it's "not a thing this integration can do" — don't add a
  speculative attempt here the way TikTok/Pinterest have one.

### Schedule

`.github/workflows/carousel-post.yml`, Tuesday and Friday at 16:00 UTC — twice
a week per Dev's request. Placeholder day/time, same status as every other
schedule in this repo (14:00 UTC daily-reel, 18:00 UTC every-2-days
hot-takes) — deliberately offset from both so nothing lands in the same
window, revisit once there's engagement data.

### Open / not yet verified

- **Never run end-to-end against live accounts as of this writing.** Every
  piece was checked individually (image prep verified by eye on real c01
  assets, Buffer's image asset schema confirmed from current docs, Meta's
  carousel/multi-photo request shapes confirmed from current docs, all new
  Python compiles and the c-series filter was confirmed to isolate exactly 50
  pairs from the 57 on disk), but no real post has actually gone out yet. The
  first scheduled or manually-dispatched run IS the real test — check actual
  post ids on all platforms attempted, the same discipline already applied to
  every other pipeline in this repo before it was trusted.
- TikTok and Pinterest publish paths are speculative, see above — don't be
  surprised if the first run needs a follow-up fix to
  `publish_image_carousel_to_buffer` once a real response body is seen.
- Caption content is identical across every platform attempted, same known
  tradeoff already recorded for the main daily pipeline — not platform-native.
